name.text: CB01 — Why the Node Uses a Public Subnet

questiontext.text: Your VPC has two public subnets and two private subnets, and it has no NAT Gateway. Your EKS worker node runs in a public subnet with a public IP address, while the RDS database runs in the private subnets. Why does the node need to run in a public subnet instead of a private one?

answer.text: Without a NAT Gateway, a node in a private subnet has no route to the internet, so it could not pull images from ECR or reach AWS APIs.
Amazon EKS only supports worker nodes that are placed in public subnets.
RDS only accepts database connections from resources that are in public subnets.
Private subnets are billed by the hour, while public subnets are free to use.

name.text: CB02 — Passing an Ephemeral Password to RDS

questiontext.text: In your infra/20-data stack, you read the database password from Secrets Manager with an ephemeral "aws_secretsmanager_secret_version" block, and you want to pass it to aws_db_instance without it ever being saved in Terraform state. Which approach works?

answer.text: Pass it to the write-only argument password_wo together with password_wo_version, because ephemeral values are only allowed in write-only arguments, which are never saved to state.
Pass it to the normal password argument, because Terraform automatically encrypts any value that comes from an ephemeral block.
Pass it to the normal password argument and mark that argument as sensitive, which keeps the value out of the state file.
Pass only the username, because RDS reads the matching password from Secrets Manager on its own once it knows the user.

questiontext.text: You create a brand-new RDS for PostgreSQL 17 instance, and your security groups correctly allow port 5432 from the EKS node. When the backend pod starts, it logs the error no pg_hba.conf entry … no encryption and cannot connect. What is causing the error?

answer.text: RDS for PostgreSQL 15 and later requires TLS by default (rds.force_ssl = 1), and the backend is trying to connect without encryption.
Port 5432 is actually blocked, so the connection falls back to an unencrypted port that RDS rejects.
The password that External Secrets synced into the cluster does not match the password set on the database.
The DB subnet group uses public subnets, and RDS refuses connections to instances placed in public subnets.

name.text: CB04 — Too Many Pods on One Node

questiontext.text: Your single t3.medium node reports a pod capacity of 17, and new pods are stuck in Pending with the reason Too many pods. Which fix actually raises the node's limit to 110 pods?

answer.text: Set ENABLE_PREFIX_DELEGATION=true on the VPC CNI add-on before the node group is created, then re-create the cluster stack so a new node joins with it turned on.
Set ENABLE_PREFIX_DELEGATION=true on the running add-on, and the existing node picks up the new limit within a few minutes.
Lower the HPA's maxReplicas, so the cluster creates fewer pods in the first place.
Give every pod smaller memory requests, so more pods fit on the node.

name.text: CB05 — The Annotation Came After the Pod

questiontext.text: A test pod is already running with the external-secrets ServiceAccount. You then add the eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn annotation to that ServiceAccount. Inside the same pod, the AWS CLI still reports Unable to locate credentials. Why does the pod still have no credentials?

answer.text: The role variables and token are only injected into pods created after the annotation is added, so the pod has to be re-created.
IAM needs up to an hour before it trusts a ServiceAccount that has just been annotated.
The cluster does not get an OIDC provider until the first annotated pod starts.
The node's IAM role blocks the pod from using any other role.

name.text: CB06 — Pointing at a Forbidden Secret

questiontext.text: The db-credentials ExternalSecret has been syncing without problems. You change its remoteRef.key to a secret that the IRSA role is not allowed to read, and you apply the change. What happens to the existing Kubernetes Secret called db-credentials?

answer.text: The Secret keeps its current data, and the ExternalSecret's status reports the access-denied error.
External Secrets deletes the Secret, because the Secret is owned by the ExternalSecret.
External Secrets empties the Secret's keys, so the app cannot keep using stale credentials.
External Secrets falls back to the node's IAM role and syncs the new secret anyway.

name.text: CB07 — The Password Changed but the App Didn't

questiontext.text: The database password is rotated in Secrets Manager. External Secrets refreshes, and kubectl get secret db-credentials now shows the new value. The backend loads this Secret with envFrom, but it still fails to log in to the database. What do you need to do?

answer.text: Restart the backend Deployment, because pods only read their environment variables when they start.
Lower the ExternalSecret's refreshInterval, so the new password is picked up sooner.
Restart the External Secrets Operator, so it pushes the new value into the running pods.
Annotate the ServiceAccount again, so IRSA issues fresh credentials to the backend.

name.text: CB08 — Which Load Balancer AWS Creates

questiontext.text: On an EKS cluster with no extra load balancer controller installed, you create a Service of type: LoadBalancer without any annotations. What kind of load balancer does AWS create for it?

answer.text: AWS creates a Classic Load Balancer, and you need the annotation service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-type: nlb to get a Network Load Balancer.
AWS creates a Network Load Balancer, because that is the default for LoadBalancer Services.
AWS creates an Application Load Balancer, because the Service carries HTTP traffic.
AWS creates nothing, because EKS cannot create load balancers without the AWS Load Balancer Controller.

name.text: CB09 — Destroying the Stacks in the Wrong Order

questiontext.text: At the end of a session, you run terraform destroy on 40-track-b-cluster before you destroy 41-track-b-platform. What is the main risk of doing it in this order?

answer.text: The NLB created by the ingress controller's Service can be left running outside Terraform, because the cluster that should delete it is already gone.
There is no risk, because the NLB is in the cluster stack's Terraform state and is destroyed along with the cluster.
Argo CD re-creates the cluster from Git as soon as it notices the cluster is missing.
The RDS database is deleted too, because it depends on the cluster's security group.

name.text: CB10 — Why the Deployment Has No replicas Field

questiontext.text: When autoscaling is turned on, your backend Deployment template leaves out the replicas field, and Argo CD manages the Deployment with self-heal turned on. Why is the replicas field left out?

answer.text: If the field were there, Argo CD would keep resetting the replica count to the value in Git, fighting the HPA's scaling decisions.
The HPA refuses to target any Deployment that has a replicas field set.
Kubernetes ignores the replicas field whenever an HPA exists, so the field is just noise.
Leaving it out frees up one pod slot on the single node.
